job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Nikhil Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My day starts at six with a run and then an hour of code before breakfast, because that's when I'm sharpest. I'm in student halls at Rowan City University doing a master's in data engineering after a computer science degree. After classes I work on a side project, a small tool that helps corner shops track their stock, and I sell it to three shops for a monthly fee. I did eight weeks last summer at a startup making payroll software. My uncle runs a small accounting practice and has been a mentor, but he can't lend money. I owe about 35,000.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected, and that the people shouting about doom were selling something. I use AI all day, and it's a good assistant, not a replacement. I'd say to my friends at the temple that hard work and a good idea still win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine, but I'd still feel the clock. Debt of 35,000 doesn't care about hype or no hype. And the openings near Rowan are few: perhaps two data jobs a year at the bank and the hospital trust. So I'd not wait for one of those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's, keep growing the shop tool to about ten shops, and apply to maybe 30 data roles including the bank. I'd also try to get my uncle's accounting clients to use the tool, since many of them are small traders. If it brought in 500 a month, that's a real dent in the rent and the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Optimistic, with a tight feeling in the chest at the end of each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your stock tool earn, and who are the shops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It earns 90 a month now from three shops. They're a spice shop, a phone repair counter and a florist near the station. They pay because the tool saves them from running out of stock, and I like the feeling that it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the point of the master's if AI stalls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me the credential and the contacts. A master's from Rowan opens doors with the bank and the hospital. But I'd not pretend I need it for the tool. I'd have built that anyway.

say: I'd say hard work and a good idea **still win**, and the doom sellers were selling something.
I'd say AI is a good assistant, not a replacement.
think: The **35,000 debt** doesn't care about hype, and the openings near Rowan are only about two data jobs a year.
I wouldn't wait for one of those.
do: Grow the shop tool from three to about **ten shops** and apply to 30 data roles.
Pitch the tool to my uncle's **accounting clients**, aiming for 500 a month.
feel: **Optimistic**, with a tight chest at the end of each month.

steps.text: Sign up seven more corner shops to the stock tool
Apply to 30 data roles, including the bank and the hospital trust
Finish the data engineering master's and keep running every morning

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time ever to start something small, if you know how to use the tools. I'd tell people that the market rewards those who move first. And I'd say that governments shouldn't clamp down so hard that only the giants can afford the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the junior coding job, the one I'd be applying for, shrinks hard. At the payroll startup, a lot of what I did was writing small features and fixing bugs, and now an AI can do half of it. A firm needs fewer of me. But a person who can start a small business with the tools, that's a different thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tool and build two more products for small traders, using AI to move fast. I'd try for 20 shops by next year and about 600 a month. I'd also look for a part-time job as a backstop, because I'm not that reckless, and I'd get my uncle to introduce me to clients in his network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a nervous edge. It's like a rollercoaster when you've chosen to sit in the front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your own project would AI do better than you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the coding. The AI writes cleaner first drafts than I do. What it can't do is know what a spice shop owner wants, which is to not run out of cardamom. I think that's where the value is, in understanding the person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle would say, be careful, don't throw away the master's. He'd also say that a man should make something of his own. He's a balance of both, and I think I am too.

I'd say rules shouldn't be so heavy that only giants can afford them.
think: The junior coding job I'd apply for **shrinks hard**, since an AI can do half my payroll startup work.

fieldNote: Nikhil sees the entry coding job shrinking but reads his edge as **knowing the customer**.

steps.text: Build two new products for small traders using AI coding tools

Learn how to use AI agents for customer support in my tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get moving, now, because the people who adapt in the first year will have the edge. I'd tell people to stop waiting for governments, and to work on the first thing they can control: their own skills and income. But I'd also say families and communities should look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be anxious. If AGI can do any thinking work in two years, the shop tool becomes something anyone can build. My edge disappears. My master's is worth less, and my debt is the same. I'd be racing a machine that doesn't sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to turn the shops into something that isn't just software, perhaps a local service where a person comes in, sets things up and looks after them. Something with trust and presence. I'd take any paying work, tutoring or repairs, and keep my costs down by moving in with my uncle for a while. I'd also contact my temple community for work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wired. Frightened and fascinated together, if that's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do on day one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd carry on as usual for a while, I think. A spice shop owner doesn't care whether his stock app is AI or not. But when anyone can make the app free, nobody pays me 30 a month. So I'd be selling trust, not code.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the shops do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start calling people. Every shop owner I know, every contact of my uncle's, and I'd offer to set up their systems in person for a fee. I'd rather be paid for turning up than for typing.

I'd also say families and communities should look after each other.
think: The shop tool becomes something anyone can build, so my **edge disappears**.
My master's is worth less and the **debt** is the same.
do: Offer **in-person setup** for shops, selling trust and presence rather than code.

S2.quote: I'd rather be paid for turning up than for typing.

steps.text: Offer shops a paid in-person setup and support visit
Move in with my uncle to cut the rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a gift for anyone who moves. I'd tell them to start something, build savings and make themselves useful to others. I'd say the market will reward those who prepare, and the rest will need help, and we should give it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd see it as a start-up window. Five years is enough to build a real business, perhaps a small company that sells and supports the new tools to traders. I'd be one of many, but I'd have a head start in my local community. I think I could be doing well by 2031, whatever AGI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's and use my uncle's contacts. I'd launch a small company, hire one or two people and pay myself a basic wage. I'd put 300 a month toward the loan until the company pays. And I'd keep learning the tools, because they change every few months, which I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Nervous, but in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years let you build?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A business that pays me, a debt under 10,000 and a few people working for me who I treat well. That's the dream. I might not make it work, but I'd like to have tried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be true at the end of them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: And a bit of time to be a good son and nephew. I've neglected both lately.

I'd tell people to start something and build savings.

steps.text: Launch a small company selling AI setups to local traders

Put 300 a month toward the loan until the company pays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the kindest version, because there's time to adjust. I'd say work hard, build something real and look after your family. I'd tell people not to fear the future, but to keep their feet on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel good, honestly. With ten years I could build the company, pay off the loan and have a family. I'd be 34 and maybe running a decent firm. I'd expect to change what the company does three times, but I'd survive that. The robots come around 2039 and I'd be thinking about how my company fits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a few years at a good firm to learn, then start my own at about 27. I'd save for a home near my uncle and my parents, and marry someone I'd met through the community. I'd keep studying the tools every day, which I enjoy. And I'd pay off the debt by 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content. Even a bit excited. It sounds like an adventure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my uncle that it's okay to be careful, and that I will be. I'd say that doing both, a steady job and a side bet, is the best way. He'd probably nod. He likes it when I sound like him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone cautious like your uncle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also tell him thank you, which I haven't done enough.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because my edge disappears and there is no time to rebuild it. What would help is a start-up loan with fair terms, apprenticeships that teach hands-on trust-based trades, and rules that stop only the giants benefiting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm safe because I'm adaptive. Being adaptive makes me quick, not safe. I'd just like a fair chance to try.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive makes me quick, not safe. I'd just like a fair chance to try.
portrait: Nikhil is 24, doing a **data engineering master's** after computer science, with 35,000 of debt and a small side business.
His stock tool earns 90 a month from three shops, and an uncle who runs an accounting practice mentors him.
He is traditional, free-market and **uses AI every day**, treating it as a daily assistant and a business opportunity.
His moods run uneasy to anxious, with calm at ten years when he expects to run his own firm.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his edge disappears and there is no time to rebuild it.
whatWouldHelp: He wants a **fair start-up loan**, hands-on apprenticeships in trust-based trades and rules that don't favour only giants.
